messages.body_plain:
On 01/04/2014 06:14 AM, Chester Kam wrote:
> Hi all,

> |HS.model<-  ' visual =~ NA*c(a1,a2)*x1 + c(a3,a4)*x2 + c(a5,a6)*x3

The rule is: only one modifier per term. The 'terms' -on the right hand
side (rhs)- are x1, x2 and x3. 'Modifiers' are everything before the '*'
operator. So

NA*c(a1,a2)*x1

is not valid. BUT, you can have the same term multiple times on the rhs,
each time with a different modifier. For example, you can write:

visual =~ c(a1,a2)*x1 + c(a3,a4)*x2 + c(a5,a6)*x3 + c(NA,NA)*x1

The 'x1' term appears twice. The first time with the labels, the second
time with the 'NA' vector.

Yves.

Principles from regression apply here.  (Cohen, Cohen, West and Aiken's (2003) regression text is my favorite.)  As to interpretation, think of your equation as:

Y = intercept + other predictors + b1*woody + b2*peren + error

Since woody and peren are 0-1 variables, their impact is to raise or lower the intercept--you might rewrite the equation as:

Y = intercept + b1*woody + b2*peren + other predictoprs + error

Where the condition is "herbaceous" (your baseline), then woody and peren are both 0 and drop out of the equation.  So then "intercept" is the value of Y for the "herbaceous" condition, when all other predictors are also 0.  (If you are not modeling mean structures, then this is simply the 0 point for Y.)  The b1 and b2 coefficients show the increase in the value of Y, as compared to the "herbaceous" state, when the state is actually "woody" or "peren."  If you do not have interactions, then, b1 and b2 show the increase in Y for each of those states, versus the baseline state, with the other predictors "held constant."
     If there are no interactions, you can estimate the combined effect of this "research factor" by the incremental R2 for Y, comparing a model without these dummy predictors with a model that includes these dummy predictors.
--Ed Rigdon

Q1: Say I have the following, very simple model (true.mod in my example). When I use simulateData() I can specify certain level of skewness but let the kurtosis take any value like this:

true.mod <- 'x1 ~~ 0.5*x2
             x1 ~~ 0.5*x3

datum <- simulateData(true.mod, sample.nobs=1000, kurtosis=c(3,3,3))
Error in ValeMaurelli1983(n = sample.nobs[g], COR = cov2cor(COV), skewness = skewness,  :
  skewness has wrong length

Why does this happen? Is this because of how the Vale&Maurelli1983 method works? Is there anyway to specify the kurtosis but let the skewness be freely estimated in lavaan?

Q2: (this will use the psych package just for the describe() function). While I was playing around with some toy simulation examples, I wanted to see how accurately does simulateData() matches the values I give it for skewness/kurtosis (so the skewness/kurtosis parameters in the population). If I run a small simulation like this:

#true model
true.mod <- 'x1 ~~ 0.5*x2
             x1 ~~ 0.5*x3
             x2 ~~ 0.5*x3'

reps <- 1000

#vectors to store the results
x1s <- double(reps)
x2s <- double(reps)
x3s <- double(reps)

#simulation loop
for (i in 1:reps) {
datum <- simulateData(true.mod, sample.nobs=1000, skewness=c(3,3,3))

x1s[i] <- describe(datum)$skew[1]
x2s[i] <- describe(datum)$skew[2]
x3s[i] <- describe(datum)$skew[3]
}

#they should be close to 3
> mean(x1s)
[1] 2.920994
> mean(x2s)
[1] 2.9537
> mean(x3s)
[1] 2.91432

I can see it recovers the population values quite nicely. Not too surprising, of course, since it's sample size of 1000 with 1000 repetitions (I'm sure for other people running this code it'll change but it's within the ballpark).

             x1 ~~ 0.5*x3
             x2 ~~ 0.5*x3'

x2s <- double(reps)

x2k <- double(reps)
x3k <- double(reps)

x1s[i] <- describe(datum)$skew[1]
x2s[i] <- describe(datum)$skew[2]

}

> mean(x1s)
[1] 1.600354
> mean(x2s)
[1] 1.602386
> mean(x3s)
[1] 1.592869

#shold be close to 3
> mean(x1k)
[1] 2.96485
> mean(x2k)
[1] 2.366576
> mean(x3k)
[1] 1.747734
>

The skewness is almost half of what it should be! And only one estimate of sample kurtosis (x1) is somewhat closer to  its true population value of 3! Why? Is this beacuse of how lavaan implements ValeMaurelli1983() or is this a drawback of the method itself?

Thanks!

When data is missing, there is no (unique) observed covariance matrix.
But we can estimate it, using maximum likelihood (and without losing any
data). This is where the EM algorithm comes in. The result is an
estimated covariance matrix that is indeed stored in
@Sampl...@missing.h1[[1]]$sigma, and it is this one that is used to
compute the covariance-based residuals.

Yves.

Dear all,

I am running some multigroup CFA and SEM analyses with Lavaan "as such", Lavaan mimicking EQS, and Lavaan mimicking Mplus.

Not surprisingly, the fit values that the three options yield are pretty similar, except for the RMSEA. Each time the Lavaan "as such" and the "mimic Mplus" options give an RMSEA that is about three times as large as the one that the "mimic EQS" option gives (e.g., 0.036 versus 0.012). It seems to me that something went wrong. I would be very grateful if someone could explain the large difference in RMSEA to me, and tell me which version I can best adhere to. One thing that might be relevant is that the number of groups is equal to nine (three^2) in my analyses.

Kind regards,
Ivo van der Lans

> large as the one that the "mimic EQS" option gives (e.g., 0.036 versus

 From the source (lav_fit_measures.R), and slightly simplifying:

if(object@Options$mimic %in% c("Mplus", "lavaan")) {
     RMSEA <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/df - 1/N, 0) ) ) * sqrt(G)
} else {
     RMSEA <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/df - 1/N, 0) ) )
}

So both lavaan and Mplus multiply by sqrt(G) (G is the number of
groups), while EQS does not do so. When in doubt, I would trust lavaan ;-)

The formula for multiple group setting is given by Steiger:

Steiger, JH (1998). A note on multiple sample extensions of the RMSEA
fit index. Structural Equation Modling, 5(4), 411-419..

Yves.

" (for the current version of lavaan, 0.5-14): as

very, very sensitive to starting values. "

The good news is that there's a quick and easy way to get good starting values. Just estimate the model without the equality constrain in place (e.g. in the above model take out the mult == mult1 line). Then use the results of that model as starting values for the constrained model (using the start option, which can take a lavaan object as an argument).

Eric--
     A factor derives its variance from its indicators, unless the variance is assigned directly (say, through standardization).  You must always do something to set the scale (that is, the variance) of your factors.  There are good statistical reason to use reference variables (set one indicator's loading to 1) rather than standardizing factors.  When indicators are ordinal, their own variance is arbitrary, so many packages will scale indicator variance to 1.
     I'm sorry, I got a little confused previously and made an incorrect connection.  Here is what happens.  You have an ordinal indicator y, and y's variance is arbitrarily scaled to 1.  It loads on factor f.  Then you have an equation like:
y = 1 * f + e
if you make y the factor's reference variable.  Here, e is "error."
Let's assume that y, f and e all have means of 0, and f and e are orthogonal.  Then this equation implies:
Variance(y) = 1 squared * Variance(f) + Variance(e)
or
1 = 1 squared * Variance(f) + Variance(e)
or
1 = Variance(f) + Variance(e)
or
Variance(f) = 1 - Variance(e)
and that is where the variance of the factor comes from, if you don't standardize the factor.
--Ed Rigdon
or
Variance(f) = Variance(f) + Variance(e)
